en.title: Religious Studies: the whole course
en.short: What Religious Studies covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Religious Studies is the academic study of religions as human and social phenomena. It examines beliefs, practices, texts, communities and institutions, and it uses history, philosophy, sociology, anthropology and literary study as tools. It is not the same as religious instruction. It does not ask you to join a tradition or to accept its truth claims. It asks you to describe, compare and explain, and to do so accurately and fairly.

The field covers living traditions such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Sikhism, Chinese and Japanese traditions, and the indigenous religions of Africa. It also studies how religion shapes, and is shaped by, society, politics, law, culture and the mind. Scholars differ on how religion should be defined, and some argue the category itself is a modern invention. You will meet those debates rather than one settled answer.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, Religious Studies is usually a BA taken over about four years, with early years on foundational courses and later years on the traditions and thematic topics. Colleges of education prepare teachers and award the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE). In the United Kingdom a bachelor’s degree is commonly three years. Ghana and Kenya have their own structures.

Postgraduate study usually means a master’s degree, such as an MA or an MPhil, then a PhD by research and thesis. Some universities require a dissertation at master’s level; others offer taught modules only.

Whatever the pattern, expect lectures, tutorials or seminars, essays, and a final-year project. Source and language skills matter, because many traditions are studied through translated texts, and translation choices affect interpretation.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course begins with the question of what the field is, then key concepts: sacred, myth, ritual and symbol. Classical and modern theories of religion follow, from thinkers such as Tylor, Durkheim, Weber and Freud to later critics. Then come the traditions: religious life in Africa, Hinduism, Buddhism, Chinese and Japanese traditions, Judaism, Islam, Christianity, and Sikhism with new religious movements.

The core stage turns to themes rather than traditions. You study religion through sociology, culture and psychology; sacred texts and interpretation; ritual, worship and liturgy; ethics; philosophy of religion; politics; law and human rights; interfaith dialogue and pluralism; science; development and the environment; gender and sexuality; religion in Nigeria; and research methods.

At master’s level the work becomes methodological: advanced theory, the methods and debates of comparative religion, dissertation methods, and frontier topics such as religion, media and globalisation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn each tradition on its own terms before comparing. Know its main texts, key figures, calendar, forms of worship and internal divisions. Then compare, and say clearly what you are comparing and why.

Read primary texts in translation alongside a good introduction, and note who translated and when. Use the vocabulary of the field precisely: a myth is not a false story, and a ritual is not merely an empty habit.

Write with dates and places. Religions change, and a practice in one country or century may differ in another. When you cite a scholar, give the claim and one criticism of it. Keep a glossary, and revise by explaining each topic aloud in plain words.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often describe a tradition using the vocabulary of another tradition, or treat one branch as the whole. Another common fault is presenting a contested definition, such as the sacred or religion itself, as settled.

Some write as believers or as critics rather than as students, and the work loses balance. Others confuse the study of religion with religious instruction, or assume that explaining a belief explains it away.

In research, a frequent weakness is a sample or method that cannot support the conclusion, or quoting a source without checking the translation. Give a date and place for every claim about a living community, and check current official sources for anything about law, policy or institutions.

keyPoints: Religious Studies describes, compares and explains religions; it does not instruct or judge them.
Definitions of religion and of the sacred are contested, so learn the debates, not one answer.
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and institution; check your own handbook.
Study each tradition on its own terms before comparing it with another.
Give a date and place with any claim about a living religious community.
Name the scholar and one criticism whenever you use a theory of religion.

en.title: What Is Religious Studies?
en.short: Defining religion, distinguishing religious studies from theology, and the main academic approaches.

sections.heading: Defining religion
sections.text:
There is no single agreed definition of religion. Substantive definitions say what religion is, such as belief in a god or gods, but they fit some traditions poorly, including some Buddhist traditions. Functional definitions say what religion does, such as binding a community or giving meaning, but they can stretch to movements not usually called religions. Scholars therefore state a working definition.

Religious studies is the academic, comparative and descriptive study of religions: their beliefs, practices, texts, institutions and histories, using evidence and reasoned argument.

sections.heading: Religious studies and theology
sections.text:
Theology is disciplined reflection from inside a tradition, asking what is true or orthodox for believers. Religious studies asks what people believe and do, how traditions developed, and how they compare; it does not settle whether a claim is true. This is sometimes called methodological agnosticism: the researcher neither affirms nor denies religious truth in the analysis.

A student’s own faith, or lack of it, is neither required nor a disqualification. The discipline asks for fairness, evidence and honesty about one’s position.

sections.heading: Main approaches
sections.text: Phenomenology describes religious experience and practice as it appears to believers, setting judgement aside; epoché is the term for this bracketing. It can underplay power and social context. Sociology studies religion in groups and institutions, asking how religion shapes society and is shaped by it. Anthropology uses long fieldwork and participant observation, called ethnography, to understand religion in everyday life. Psychology studies religious experience, motivation and development in individuals. History of religions sets traditions in time and place, using dated sources and historical criticism. Most good work combines several approaches.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Amina, a first-year student, wants to understand why a Lagos church and a Kano mosque both gather weekly. She attends both, takes notes, interviews leaders and reads each community’s texts. She reports what members say and how the gatherings are organised. She does not judge which is true. Her work is descriptive, comparative and evidence-based.

keyPoints: There is no single agreed definition of religion; scholars state a working definition.
Religious studies is descriptive and comparative, using evidence and reasoned argument.
Theology reflects from inside a tradition; religious studies does not settle truth claims.
Methodological agnosticism means neither affirming nor denying religious truth in analysis.
Phenomenology, sociology, anthropology, psychology and history of religions are distinct approaches.
A student’s personal belief or unbelief is neither required nor disqualifying.

en.title: Key Concepts: Sacred, Myth, Ritual and Symbol
en.short: Defines sacred and profane, myth, ritual, symbol, belief, community and experience for comparison.

sections.heading: Sacred and profane
sections.text: The sacred is what a community sets apart as powerful, meaningful and worthy of respect. The profane is ordinary, everyday life. Emile Durkheim and Mircea Eliade both use the pair, but differently: Durkheim links the sacred to society’s collective life, while Eliade contrasts sacred space with ordinary space. Some traditions do not divide life so sharply. Use the pair as a question, not a ranking: what is set apart here, and by whom?

sections.heading: Myth and symbol
sections.text: In religious studies, a myth is a sacred story a community tells to explain origins, identity or duty. It is not simply a false story. A symbol is an object, word, gesture or image that points beyond itself and carries meaning for a group. A cross, a crescent or a calabash can be a symbol, but meaning depends on context and use. One symbol may carry several meanings, and different traditions may read the same symbol differently.

sections.heading: Ritual, belief and community
sections.text: A ritual is a patterned action, often repeated, that marks time, status or relationship with the sacred. It may be public or private, formal or informal. Belief is a conviction held by a person or group; it may be stated in creeds or carried in practice. Community is the group that shares, transmits and argues over a tradition. Experience is the felt side of religion: awe, guilt, comfort or wonder. Scholars interpret reports of experience; they do not treat them as proof.

sections.heading: Comparing without judging
sections.text: A simple invented case shows the method. A student compares a Sunday communion service in a Lagos church, a Friday prayer in a Lagos mosque and a family pouring a drink at an ancestral shrine. She asks: what is set apart? What story is told? What actions repeat? What symbols appear? Who belongs? What do people say they feel? She records each answer in the tradition’s own words, notes differences, and avoids saying one is higher or truer. The vocabulary helps her compare, not rank.

keyPoints: The sacred is what a community sets apart as powerful and worthy of respect; the profane is ordinary life.
A myth is a sacred story that explains origins, identity or duty, not simply a false story.
A ritual is a patterned, often repeated action that marks time, status or relationship with the sacred.
A symbol points beyond itself and carries meaning that depends on context and use.
Belief, community and experience describe conviction, shared transmission and felt religion.
Comparative study uses these terms as questions and records each tradition in its own words without ranking.

en.title: Theories of Religion: Classical and Modern
en.short: Classical and modern theories of religion, from Tylor and Durkheim to cognitive approaches.

sections.heading: Evolution and origins
sections.text: E. B. Tylor (1871) argued that religion began in animism, the belief that spirits inhabit bodies and things. James G. Frazer placed magic, religion and science in an evolutionary sequence in The Golden Bough. Both were intellectualist: they thought religion was early people’s attempt to explain the world. Later scholars reject simple stages and note that such origin theories are speculative.

sections.heading: Society and psyche
sections.text: Émile Durkheim (1912) treated religion as a social fact. He defined the sacred as things set apart and forbidden, and the profane as ordinary life. In totemism, where a clan treats an animal or plant as its sacred emblem, he saw society worshipping itself, and rituals producing collective effervescence, shared emotional energy. Sigmund Freud saw religion as an illusion and a wish for protection, linked in Totem and Taboo to guilt and the father. Critics say both reduce religion to something else.

sections.heading: Experience and the sacred
sections.text: Rudolf Otto (1917) described the numinous as a feeling of mystery, awe and fascination, mysterium tremendum et fascinans. He insisted it is non-rational and cannot be fully expressed. Mircea Eliade spoke of homo religiosus, a religious human, and of hierophany, a manifestation of the sacred. He used axis mundi for a centre that orders space. Critics ask whether such experience is universal or shaped by culture.

sections.heading: Modern approaches
sections.text: Functionalists such as Bronislaw Malinowski and A. R. Radcliffe-Brown ask what religion does for society: it comforts, explains, and reinforces norms. Social theories ask how religion builds meaning and relates to power. Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann treat religion as a socially constructed world; Karl Marx called it the opium of the people, and Max Weber studied how beliefs shape action. Cognitive theories explain religion through ordinary mental systems. Stewart Guthrie argues that people over-detect agents; Pascal Boyer says counterintuitive ideas spread because they are memorable. A harvest ritual may strengthen solidarity (Durkheim), feel awe-inspiring (Otto), and be remembered because it mixes ordinary and extraordinary claims (cognitive theory). These views differ on what religion basically is: a social bond, a psychological need, an encounter with the sacred, or a by-product of the mind.

keyPoints: Tylor and Frazer gave evolutionary, intellectualist accounts of religion’s origin, which later scholars treat with caution.
Durkheim saw religion as a social fact that marks the sacred and binds people through collective effervescence.
Otto stressed the numinous as awe and mystery, while Eliade stressed hierophany and sacred space.
Freud treated religion as an illusion rooted in psychological wishes and guilt.
Functionalist and social theories ask what religion does for society and how it builds meaning and power.
Cognitive theories explain religion through ordinary mental biases such as agency detection and memory for counterintuitive ideas.

en.title: Religious Life in Africa: Indigenous Traditions
en.short: African indigenous beliefs about God, spirits, ancestors, divination, sacrifice and rites of passage.

sections.heading: One religion or many?
sections.text: African indigenous religions are the traditions of African peoples before and alongside Islam and Christianity. The label African Traditional Religion (ATR) is used by scholars, but many adherents do not use it. There is no single founder, scripture or central authority. Some scholars see a family of religions with shared features; others stress that each society has its own religion. The debate matters because a single label can hide real variety.

sections.heading: God, spirits and ancestors
sections.text: Many traditions speak of a Supreme Being, often a creator who is powerful and sometimes distant. Below this being are divinities or spirits linked to nature, places or human needs. Ancestors are deceased relatives who remain part of family life; people may honour them, ask their help or fear their displeasure. Beliefs differ widely. Some traditions treat the sacred as part of everyday life rather than a separate sphere.

sections.heading: Divination and sacrifice
sections.text: Divination is a way of seeking hidden knowledge or guidance, usually through a trained specialist. It may explain illness, misfortune or the right time for a journey. Sacrifice is an offering to God, spirits or ancestors. It can be food, drink, an animal or a gift, and it may express thanks, ask for help, cleanse a wrong or restore relationships. Not every offering involves killing an animal. Meanings and rules vary by society.

sections.heading: Rites of passage
sections.text: Rites of passage mark changes in a person’s life, such as birth, initiation into adulthood, marriage and death. They often separate the person from ordinary life, teach them a new role, and welcome them back. An invented example: a farming family consults a diviner about a sick child; the diviner names a neglected ancestor; the family makes a small offering and performs a welcome rite. The case shows how divination, sacrifice and family religion can connect.

keyPoints: African indigenous religions are many local traditions, not one unified religion with a founder or scripture.
The term African Traditional Religion is a scholarly label, and its use is debated.
Many traditions describe a Supreme Being, lesser spirits or divinities, and ancestors.
Divination seeks hidden knowledge or guidance through specialists.
Sacrifice is an offering that can give thanks, petition, cleanse or restore relationships.
Rites of passage mark birth, initiation, marriage and death, and they vary across societies.

en.title: Hinduism: Beliefs, Texts and Practice
en.short: Dharma, karma, samsara, moksha; Vedas, Upanishads, epics; bhakti, caste, Vedanta, worship and festivals.

sections.heading: Core ideas
sections.text: Hinduism is a family of traditions, not one system with a single founder or authority. Dharma means right order, duty and fitting conduct; it varies with life stage, role and situation. Karma is action and its consequences, across this life or many. Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Moksha is liberation from that cycle. Schools differ on its nature: union with ultimate reality or closeness to a personal God. Karma, jnana (knowledge) and bhakti (devotion) are paths.

sections.heading: Texts and schools
sections.text: The Vedas are four ancient collections: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva. Hindus call them shruti, 'that which was heard', and pass them on orally. The Upanishads are philosophical texts closing the Vedic corpus; they discuss brahman, ultimate reality, and atman, the self. The epics Mahabharata and Ramayana tell divine and heroic stories. The Bhagavad Gita, part of the Mahabharata, treats duty, devotion and liberation. Six schools include Vedanta, which interprets the Upanishads. Vedanta has rival readings: Advaita teaches non-duality; Vishishtadvaita teaches qualified non-dualism; Dvaita teaches dualism.

sections.heading: Worship and devotion
sections.text: Bhakti is loving devotion to a chosen deity. Vaishnavas focus on Vishnu and his avatars, such as Krishna and Rama; Shaivas on Shiva; Shaktas on the Goddess. In puja, worshippers offer light, water, food or flowers before a murti, an image or form of the deity, and receive prasad, blessed food. Home shrines are common. Festivals include Diwali, Holi, Navaratri and Ganesh Chaturthi. Many follow lunar calendars, and dates vary by region and year, so check local sources.

sections.heading: Caste and modern life
sections.text: Caste is complex. Varna names four broad social categories; jati names many birth groups. Critics, including B. R. Ambedkar, condemned caste oppression. India’s constitution abolishes untouchability and bans caste discrimination, though inequality persists. Hindus live worldwide. Reform movements, education and law have changed practice, and debates continue over caste, gender and temple authority. A family may keep a home shrine and attend a temple, while younger members interpret dharma in relation to work and equality.

keyPoints: Hinduism is a family of traditions with no single founder or authority.
Dharma, karma, samsara and moksha describe duty, action, rebirth and liberation.
The Vedas are shruti; the Upanishads and Vedanta interpret ultimate reality and the self.
Bhakti devotion, puja and festivals are central in many Hindu lives.
Caste includes varna and jati; critics condemn oppression, and India’s constitution bans caste discrimination.
Vedanta schools such as Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita disagree about unity and difference.

en.title: Buddhism: The Buddha’s Life and Paths to Liberation
en.short: The Buddha’s life, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, karma, monasticism, meditation and the three main traditions.

sections.heading: The Buddha’s life
sections.text:
Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal, into a noble family of the Sakya clan. Tradition says he saw four sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering seeker. He left his palace, tried severe austerity, then took a middle way between indulgence and self-torture. He woke to enlightenment (bodhi) at Bodh Gaya and gave his first teaching at Sarnath, dying at Kusinara.

His dates are disputed; most scholars place him in the fifth century BCE. These stories come from later devotional biographies, not from contemporary records.

sections.heading: Four Noble Truths
sections.text:
The Four Noble Truths say that life involves dukkha (suffering, or unsatisfactoriness); that its origin is tanha (craving); that it can cease (nirodha, nirvana); and that there is a way to that cessation.

The way is the Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. These eight are often grouped under wisdom, ethics and meditation.

sections.heading: Karma, monks and meditation
sections.text:
Karma means intentional action that shapes future experience. Because Buddhism denies a permanent self (anatta), rebirth is not a soul moving between bodies but a causal continuity, explained by dependent origination. The sangha, the monastic community, lives by the Vinaya rules and depends on lay alms. In Sri Lanka, many lay people mark full-moon Poya days; some take the eight precepts and offer food at a temple.

Meditation is samatha (calming) and vipassana (insight), with mindfulness of breathing and metta (loving-kindness).

sections.heading: Three traditions
sections.text: Theravada, meaning way of the elders, keeps the Pali canon and the ideal of the arhat; it spread to Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia. Mahayana adds the bodhisattva ideal, one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings, and the teaching of emptiness (sunyata); it spread to China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Vajrayana, often counted as part of Mahayana, uses tantra, mantra and visualisation, and is dominant in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.

keyPoints: The Buddha’s biography comes from later devotional texts, and his dates are disputed.
The Four Noble Truths teach that dukkha arises from craving and can cease.
The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom, ethics and meditation.
Buddhism denies a permanent self, so rebirth is causal continuity, not a soul moving on.
The sangha lives by the Vinaya rules and is supported by lay alms.
Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana differ in ideals, texts and regions of Asia.

en.title: Chinese and Japanese Traditions: Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto
en.short: Confucian ethics and ritual, Daoist Dao and wu wei, Shinto kami and shrines, and their overlap.

sections.heading: Confucian ethics and ritual
sections.text:
Confucianism comes from the teachings of Kongzi (Confucius), recorded in the Analects. Its central ideas include ren, humaneness or goodwill; li, ritual propriety and proper conduct; and xiao, filial piety, the duty of children to parents.

The family is the first school of ethics, and respect extends to ancestors and elders. The ideal person, the junzi, acts with moral seriousness and courtesy. Ritual here means more than ceremonies: it includes greetings, mourning, offerings and everyday manners that shape character and social harmony.

sections.heading: Daoist Dao and wu wei
sections.text:
Daoism is associated with the Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, and the Zhuangzi. The Dao is the way or source of order that cannot be fully captured in words.

Daoists value ziran, naturalness or spontaneity. Wu wei, often translated as non-action, means acting without force or strain, not doing nothing. A ruler who practises wu wei governs lightly; a person who yields like water may achieve more. Religious Daoism also has deities, priests and rituals, so it is not one uniform tradition.

sections.heading: Shinto, kami and shrines
sections.text:
Shinto is a modern label for Japanese traditions focused on kami, sacred powers or spirits found in places, natural forces, ancestors and revered figures.

Shrines, called jinja, mark kami presence; a torii gate often frames the approach. Worshippers purify themselves, make offerings, bow and clap. Festivals, or matsuri, carry kami through streets and renew community ties. Shinto has no single founder or closed scripture, though old myths appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Practice varies locally.

sections.heading: Overlapping traditions
sections.text:
These traditions are not exclusive brands. In China, Confucian family ethics, Daoist ritual and Buddhist practice often coexist.

In Japan, many families visit a Shinto shrine at New Year and hold Buddhist funerals, while Confucian ideas about respect for elders shape education and manners. A household may use different traditions for different needs without declaring one identity. Scholars therefore speak of lived religion and syncretism, meaning the mixing of elements, rather than separate compartments.

keyPoints: Confucianism centres on ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety) and xiao (filial piety).
The Dao is the ineffable way or source of order, and wu wei means acting without forcing.
Kami are sacred powers or spirits honoured at Shinto shrines through purification, offerings and festivals.
Shinto has no single founder or closed scripture, and local practice varies.
In East Asia, Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist and Shinto elements often overlap in lived religion.
Syncretism means the mixing of religious elements, so membership is not always exclusive.

en.title: Judaism: Covenant, Torah and Community
en.short: Covenant, Torah and Talmud, beliefs, festivals, synagogue prayer, calendar, history and modern Jewish movements.

sections.heading: Covenant and beliefs
sections.text:
Judaism teaches that one God made a covenant, a binding agreement, with Israel. The Bible describes covenants with Abraham and, at Sinai, with Moses and the people. The covenant brings mitzvot, commands, and a way of life. Tradition often calls Israel chosen, meaning set apart for covenant and responsibility; interpretations differ.

Central beliefs include God’s unity, Torah’s authority and hope for redemption. Belief and practice are joined, so Judaism is often called a way of life, not only doctrines.

sections.heading: Torah and Talmud
sections.text:
Torah can mean the five books of Moses, the Pentateuch, the scroll read in synagogue, or teaching more broadly. It is central to Jewish life. The Talmud records rabbinic debate on law, ethics and practice. It joins the Mishnah, compiled around 200 CE, with the Gemara, commentary on it.

Halakhah means Jewish law, the path of practice. Study is a religious act, and interpreters argue from text to application. Judaism therefore has a strong tradition of commentary and disagreement.

sections.heading: Synagogue and calendar
sections.text:
The synagogue is a house of prayer, study and assembly. A rabbi teaches and guides but is not a priest. Services include the Shema. Many prayers need a minyan, a quorum of ten adults; Orthodox Judaism counts ten men, while other movements include women.

The calendar is lunar with solar adjustment, adding a leap month in some years. Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Festivals include Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Pesach, Shavuot, Hanukkah and Purim. A student who keeps Shabbat may prepare food before sunset, attend synagogue and avoid work until nightfall; practice varies by movement.

sections.heading: History and movements
sections.text:
Ancient Israelite religion centred on the Jerusalem Temple. Exile and the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE pushed Judaism toward Torah, synagogue and rabbinic leadership.

Modern movements arose in Europe and America from the nineteenth century onward. Orthodox Judaism treats Torah and halakhah as binding. Reform Judaism emphasises autonomy and adaptation. Conservative or Masorti Judaism seeks continuity with change, and Reconstructionist Judaism sees Judaism as an evolving civilisation.

keyPoints: Judaism centres on a covenant between one God and Israel, expressed through mitzvot and a way of life.
Torah means the five books of Moses, the synagogue scroll or teaching; Talmud records rabbinic debate on law and practice.
Halakhah is Jewish law and practice, developed through study and interpretation.
The synagogue is a house of prayer, study and assembly, and many prayers require a minyan.
The Jewish calendar is lunar with solar adjustment; Shabbat and festivals shape community life.
After the Temple’s destruction, rabbinic Judaism developed, and modern movements differ over how far Torah and halakhah are binding.

en.title: Islam: Qur’an, Faith and Practice
en.short: Muhammad’s life, the Qur’an and Hadith, the pillars, sharia schools, Sunni and Shia Islam.

sections.heading: Muhammad and the revelation
sections.text:
Muhammad was born in Mecca, in present-day Saudi Arabia, around 570 CE. Muslims believe that from about 610 CE he received revelations from God through the angel Jibril (Gabriel). He preached in Mecca, then moved to Medina in 622, the year that begins the Islamic calendar, and died there in 632.

Muslims regard him as the last prophet, a human messenger and not divine. His move to Medina, the Hijra, marks the start of a community with its own laws and leadership, not only a set of beliefs.

sections.heading: Qur’an and Hadith
sections.text:
The Qur’an is the collection of these revelations in Arabic, arranged in 114 suras (chapters). Muslims hold it to be the word of God, and its recitation is itself an act of worship.

The Hadith are separate reports of what the Prophet said and did, gathered in collections such as those of al-Bukhari and Muslim. Hadith and the Prophet’s practice, the sunna, guide Muslims where the Qur’an is silent. Scholars judge reports by their chain of transmission, so not every hadith carries equal weight.

sections.heading: Pillars and articles of faith
sections.text:
Sunni Muslims speak of five pillars of practice: the shahada (declaration that there is no god but God and Muhammad is his messenger), salat (five daily prayers), zakat (almsgiving), sawm (fasting in Ramadan) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca once, for those able). They also name six articles of faith: God, angels, revealed books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and divine decree.

Zakat is commonly 2.5% of savings held for a lunar year above a minimum threshold, called the nisab. On 400,000 naira above the nisab: 400,000 × 2.5% = 10,000 naira. Rates for crops and livestock differ, so check a scholar or a current manual.

sections.heading: Sharia, schools and community
sections.text:
Sharia means the path of divine guidance; fiqh is the human understanding of it. Sunni law has four classical schools, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali, which differ on details.

Shia Muslims, the other major branch, hold that leadership passed to Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, and to the Imams descended from him; Twelver Shia law follows the Ja’fari school. Muslims worship in a mosque behind an imam, gather for Friday prayer, and mark the Eids.

keyPoints: Muhammad, born in Mecca around 570 CE, received revelations from about 610 and died in Medina in 632.
The Qur’an has 114 suras and is held by Muslims to be the word of God in Arabic; Hadith report the Prophet’s words and deeds.
The five pillars are shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj; the six articles of faith cover God, angels, books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and divine decree.
Zakat is commonly 2.5% of qualifying savings above the nisab held for a lunar year: 400,000 naira gives 10,000 naira.
Sunni and Shia Muslims differ chiefly over leadership after the Prophet; Sunni law has four classical schools, Shia law the Ja’fari school.
Sharia is the divine path and fiqh the human interpretation of it, so scholars differ on details.

en.title: Christianity: Bible, Creeds and Church
en.short: Jesus, the Bible’s formation, creeds, Trinity, salvation, and the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches.

sections.heading: Jesus of Nazareth
sections.text:
Christians are named after Jesus Christ, a Jewish teacher in first-century Galilee and Judea. The four Gospels present his baptism by John, his parables and healings, his teaching about the kingdom of God, his crucifixion under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, and the disciples’ claim that God raised him from the dead.

Historians also study him as a Jew of his time, using Roman and Jewish writings alongside the Gospels. The Gospels are works of faith, not modern biographies, and they differ in detail.

sections.heading: Bible and creeds
sections.text:
The Bible has two parts. The Old Testament is the Hebrew scriptures; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add books Protestants call the Apocrypha. The New Testament has 27 books: Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation. The canon, the official list, settled over centuries; Athanasius listed these 27 in 367.

Creeds are short statements of faith. The Nicene Creed was agreed at Nicaea in 325 and completed at Constantinople in 381. The Apostles’ Creed grew from early baptismal confessions.

sections.heading: Trinity and salvation
sections.text:
The Trinity is one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, distinct yet of one being. Salvation means being rescued from sin and death and restored to God.

Accounts of how salvation works differ. Some stress victory over evil, some satisfaction for God’s honour (Anselm), some penal substitution, some moral influence (Abelard), and Orthodoxy stresses theosis, becoming like God. Luther taught justification by faith.

sections.heading: Churches and worship
sections.text:
Catholics accept the pope’s authority, seven sacraments and transubstantiation, the belief that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood. Orthodox churches are self-governing under patriarchs and stress icons and theosis. Protestants, from the sixteenth-century Reformation, stress scripture and faith and usually keep two sacraments, baptism and the Eucharist.

Worship centres on the Eucharist in Catholic and Orthodox liturgy, and on preaching in many Protestant churches. Chidinma, a student in Enugu, attends Mass, where the Eucharist is central, then a Pentecostal service of singing and sermon; both read the same Gospels.

Christianity spread from Jerusalem through Paul’s missions and early churches in Armenia and Ethiopia, and later through mission and migration.

keyPoints: The Gospels present Jesus’s teaching, death and resurrection; historians also study him as a first-century Jewish teacher.
The New Testament has 27 books, and the canon settled over several centuries.
Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Old Testament books that Protestants call the Apocrypha.
The Nicene Creed (325 and 381) and the Apostles’ Creed confess one God in three persons.
Theories of salvation differ, including Christus Victor, satisfaction, penal substitution, moral influence and theosis.
Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches affirm the same core faith in one God in three persons but differ on authority, sacraments and worship.

en.title: Sikhism and New Religious Movements
en.short: Sikh beliefs, the Gurus and Guru Granth Sahib, worship, and how scholars study new religious movements.

sections.heading: Sikh belief and the Gurus
sections.text:
Sikhism began in the Punjab with Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539). Sikhs believe in one formless God, Ik Onkar, and in karma and rebirth. Liberation comes through God’s grace, meditation on the divine name (naam simran) and honest living.

There were ten Gurus. The last, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, in 1699 and before his death in 1708 designated the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Sikhs reject caste distinctions and affirm the equality of women and men in worship.

sections.heading: Scripture and community life
sections.text:
The Guru Granth Sahib is the Sikh scripture, a collection of hymns by the Gurus and by saints from other traditions. It is treated as a living Guru: it is enthroned, opened with care and read aloud.

Worship takes place in the gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, and includes hymn singing (kirtan), prayer and a shared meal. The langar, a free community kitchen, enacts equality, since all sit together. Community life centres on sangat, the congregation, and on service (sewa).

sections.heading: New religious movements
sections.text: New religious movements (NRMs) are religious groups that have arisen recently, usually since the nineteenth century, and that differ from established traditions. Examples include the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Jehovah’s Witnesses, the Bahá’í Faith, Rastafari, Soka Gakkai and many Pentecostal and charismatic churches. The category is descriptive, not a judgement on truth.

sections.heading: Theories and the word cult
sections.text:
Sociologists use several theories. The church-sect typology, from Max Weber and Ernst Troeltsch, traces how movements settle or split. Roy Wallis classified movements as world-affirming, world-rejecting or world-accommodating. Stark and Bainbridge used a rational-choice model: movements offer rewards and compensators (promised rewards when real ones are not available). Deprivation theory links membership to social disadvantage, and conversion studies describe steps towards commitment.

The word cult is contested. It is often pejorative, and most scholars prefer NRM. The brainwashing claim is disputed; critics say it ignores members’ own reasons.

keyPoints: Sikhs believe in one God, Ik Onkar, and in karma, rebirth and liberation through grace.
There were ten Gurus; Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699.
The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as the eternal Guru and read with reverence.
The gurdwara, langar and sewa express equality and community.
New religious movements are recent groups studied descriptively, not ranked.
The word cult is pejorative and contested; brainwashing claims are disputed.

en.title: Religion and Society: Sociological Approaches
en.short: Secularisation, rational choice and market theory, and whether religion is declining or changing.

sections.heading: Secularisation
sections.text:
Secularisation is the idea that religion loses social importance as societies modernise: in law, politics, education and everyday life. Max Weber described the modern world as disenchanted, meaning that explanations no longer rest on supernatural forces. Bryan Wilson and Steve Bruce argued that industrial societies push religion into a private corner. The thesis predicts falling attendance and weaker church authority.

Critics say secularisation describes western Europe rather than a universal law. Peter Berger, once a supporter, later wrote of desecularisation, the return of religion to public life. José Casanova argued that religion can be privatised in one place and public in another.

sections.heading: Rational choice and markets
sections.text:
Rational choice theory treats people as weighing costs and benefits, including in religion. Rodney Stark and William Sims Bainbridge argued that people seek rewards, and religion offers compensators: promises of benefits that cannot be verified now, such as salvation.

Market theory, or the religious economies model, applies economics to religion. Where many groups compete freely, they work harder to attract members, so participation tends to be higher. Where one church is state-supported, it may become lazy and attendance falls. Stark and Roger Finke developed this. Critics reply that belief is not shopping and that the measures are crude.

sections.heading: Decline or change?
sections.text:
Evidence is mixed. Church attendance has fallen sharply in much of western Europe since the 1960s, yet surveys in the United States show slower decline, and Pentecostal movements are growing in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Growth in Pentecostalism is often explained by lively worship, small groups and promises of health and success. Muslim populations are also growing, mainly in Africa and Asia, partly through higher birth rates in some regions.

Consider an invented case: a Nigerian town gains three new Pentecostal churches while the older mission church empties. That is not simply decline; it is realignment. Attendance figures depend on how questions are asked, so check current national surveys and Pew Research Center reports before quoting numbers.

keyPoints: Secularisation means religion losing social importance as societies modernise.
Weber described modernity as disenchanted; Wilson and Bruce applied the thesis to industrial societies.
Berger’s desecularisation and Casanova’s public religions challenge the thesis.
Rational choice theory says people weigh religious costs and benefits, and religion offers compensators.
Market theory predicts higher participation where many religious groups compete freely.
Falling European attendance and growing Pentecostal and Muslim movements suggest change as well as decline.

en.title: Religion and Culture: Anthropological Approaches
en.short: Fieldwork, thick description, ritual and symbol, with classic ethnographic cases.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and method
sections.text: Anthropology studies religion as lived culture: practices, words and institutions. Its main method is fieldwork: long residence among people, learning their language and joining daily life. Participant observation means the researcher both joins activities and watches them. Anthropologists keep field notes, conduct interviews and compare what people say with what they do. They record emic views, insiders’ own categories, and etic analysis, the outsider’s analytical framework. Good practice needs consent and honesty about the researcher’s presence.

sections.heading: Thick description
sections.text: Clifford Geertz called thick description an account of the meaning an act has for those who perform it. A wink and a blink differ in meaning. Geertz treated religion as a cultural system of symbols shaping moods and motivations. His essay on the Balinese cockfight (1973) reads the event as a text about status and rivalry. Critics such as Talal Asad warn that ‘religion’ is a historical category, not universal, and that Geertz separated meaning from power.

sections.heading: Ritual and symbol
sections.text: Ritual is patterned action that carries meaning. A symbol is an object, word or gesture with meaning beyond itself. Victor Turner studied Ndembu rituals in Zambia and argued that symbols condense meanings and ease social tensions. Liminality names the in-between stage of rites of passage. Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), showed that ideas of dirt and purity mark social boundaries. Anthropologists ask how symbols work in context, not whether they are true.

sections.heading: Classic cases
sections.text: E. E. Evans-Pritchard’s Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande showed how Zande explanations of misfortune formed a coherent system. When a granary collapsed, witchcraft might be blamed, while the natural cause was also known. This is not a lack of reason but a different way of linking events to meaning. Such cases show that religious practice is embedded in kinship, economy and politics. Later anthropology stresses reflexivity: the researcher’s own position affects the account.

keyPoints: Fieldwork and participant observation study religion as lived practice, not only as doctrine.
Thick description links an act to the meanings it has for participants.
Rituals are patterned actions, and symbols carry meanings that must be read in context.
Evans-Pritchard showed that Zande witchcraft beliefs formed a coherent system of explanation.
Turner and Douglas showed how ritual symbols mark social tensions and boundaries.
Anthropologists now stress reflexivity and the colonial history of the discipline.

en.title: Religion and Psychology: Experience and the Mind
en.short: James, Freud and Jung on religious experience, plus conversion research and cognitive science.

sections.heading: James and experience
sections.text: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), treated religion as personal experience rather than doctrine. He collected accounts and judged them by their fruits, meaning their effects on life. He described healthy-minded religion, which dwells on goodness, and the sick soul, which feels evil deeply and may be saved by conversion. James did not decide whether experiences prove God; he studied their psychology. This pragmatic approach, judging ideas by practical consequences, shaped the field.

sections.heading: Freud and Jung
sections.text: Sigmund Freud saw religion as an illusion, a wish for a protective father and consolation against helplessness (The Future of an Illusion, 1927). He linked some ritual to obsessive behaviour, an analogy critics call reductive. Carl Jung disagreed. He posited a collective unconscious, shared inherited patterns called archetypes, and read religious symbols as expressions of psychological growth, or individuation. Freud thought religion could be outgrown; Jung thought it could heal. Neither view is settled, and many psychologists reject both claims.

sections.heading: Conversion research
sections.text: Modern research studies religious experience as reported and interpreted. Attribution theory asks what causes people give for unusual feelings: a sense of presence may be credited to God, to a dead relative or to tiredness. Conversion, a turning to a new faith or renewed commitment, is often gradual rather than sudden. A case: a student joins a fellowship after a stressful term, feels accepted, and describes the change as being born again. Researchers may explain it through social support, identity and emotion, without denying the person’s account.

sections.heading: Cognitive science
sections.text: The cognitive science of religion asks why religious ideas are common. It uses experiments and evolutionary theory. Pascal Boyer argues that beliefs spread when they mildly violate ordinary expectations, such as a being who knows everything. Justin Barrett’s work on agency detection suggests people see intention behind events. Harvey Whitehouse distinguishes imagistic rituals, rare and emotional, from doctrinal rituals, frequent and routine. Critics say such theories explain recurrence, not truth, and may underplay culture and history.

keyPoints: William James studied religious experience through its practical effects, not its truth.
Freud treated religion as an illusion rooted in wish and helplessness.
Jung saw religious symbols as expressions of the collective unconscious and individuation.
Conversion is often gradual and shaped by emotion, identity and social support.
Attribution theory studies the causes people give for unusual experiences.
Cognitive scientists explain religious ideas through ordinary thought biases, but critics say this does not settle their truth.

en.title: Sacred Texts and Methods of Interpretation
en.short: Scripture, canon, oral and written forms, and historical, literary and insider methods.

sections.heading: Scripture, oral and written
sections.text: Scripture means writings or words treated as sacred and authoritative. Its role differs. The Vedas were transmitted orally with exact recitation before being written; the Qur’an is both memorised and written; the Torah is read from a scroll in worship; Buddhist communities preserve canons in Pali and other languages. Oral performance can carry authority that a printed book does not. Written texts help fix wording, but recitation, chant and commentary keep them alive. A sacred text may be read silently, chanted, memorised or displayed.

sections.heading: Canon and authority
sections.text: Canon is a recognised list of authoritative texts. Canons form over time and differ: Jewish, Christian and Buddhist communities have different lists, and Christian canons vary among churches. Muslims treat the Qur’an as revealed scripture; hadith collections also carry authority but are not the Qur’an. Authority may lie in the text, in a community that interprets it, in tradition, or in a teacher. A text can be authoritative without being the only authority.

sections.heading: Criticism and interpretation
sections.text: Exegesis means close explanation of a text; hermeneutics is reflection on how interpretation works. Historical criticism asks about a text’s historical setting, sources, editing and first audiences. Literary criticism asks about genre, structure, narrative, rhetoric and links to other texts. Both are methods, not verdicts on faith. Example: a scholar may study a Genesis creation account alongside other ancient Near Eastern stories (historical criticism) and also analyse its repeated phrases and order (literary criticism). The insider outsider debate asks whether only believers can interpret a tradition. Insiders may know its lived meaning; outsiders may notice assumptions insiders miss. Many scholars combine both, stating their position openly.

keyPoints: Scripture is sacred and authoritative, and its role varies between traditions.
Oral recitation and memorisation can carry authority alongside written texts.
Canon is a recognised list of authoritative texts, formed over time and differing between communities.
Historical criticism studies a text’s setting, sources and editing; literary criticism studies its genre, structure and rhetoric.
The insider outsider debate asks whether only believers can interpret a tradition; many scholars combine insider knowledge with outsider methods.
Exegesis explains a text closely, while hermeneutics reflects on how interpretation works.

en.title: Ritual, Worship and Liturgy: Forms, Functions and Comparison
en.short: Ritual forms and functions, rites of passage, sacrifice, prayer, meditation, liturgy, puja, salat and African rites.

sections.heading: Ritual and function
sections.text: Ritual is patterned, repeated action performed with attention to meaning and the sacred. It may be formal or informal. It can mark time, form identity, teach beliefs, express emotion, seek healing and bind a community. Sacrifice is an offering to a sacred power, commonly food, drink or an animal; explanations include gift, communion, purification and substitute. Prayer is address to the sacred in praise, petition, confession or thanks. Meditation is disciplined attention or contemplation. Liturgy is public, usually scripted worship, such as a church service or synagogue prayer.

sections.heading: Rites of passage
sections.text: Arnold van Gennep described rites of passage as separation, liminality and incorporation. Victor Turner explored liminality, a betwixt-and-between stage. Birth, naming, initiation, marriage and death are common examples. In many African indigenous traditions, naming, initiation, marriage and funeral rites involve elders, ancestors, libation (poured drink offerings) and sacrifice; practice varies greatly and is not one system. Jewish life-cycle rites include circumcision, bar or bat mitzvah, marriage and burial. Muslim families mark birth, marriage and death with prayer and community support, though customs vary.

sections.heading: Marking sacred time
sections.text: Rituals structure daily, weekly and yearly time. Muslim salat is performed five times daily facing the qibla (the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca), with ablution and prayer cycles; Friday prayer is congregational. Jewish prayer has fixed services and Sabbath and festival liturgy. Hindu puja may be daily at a home shrine or in a temple, with offerings, mantras and darshan, the seeing and being seen by the deity. Christian worship commonly gathers on Sunday around Bible reading and Eucharist, and follows Advent, Lent and Easter; forms differ by church. African rites tie community to agricultural and life-cycle seasons.

sections.heading: Comparison and caution
sections.text: Comparison shows functions but not identical meanings. Puja, salat, Jewish prayer and Christian liturgy order time and form community, yet each tradition understands what happens differently. Some stress divine command, some communion, some remembrance. African rites are diverse. Students should not treat one tradition’s practice as the norm.

keyPoints: Rituals are patterned actions that mark time, form identity, teach beliefs and bind communities.
Rites of passage commonly move through separation, liminality and incorporation.
Sacrifice, prayer, meditation and liturgy are distinct ritual forms with overlapping functions.
Hindu puja, Jewish prayer, Christian worship and Muslim salat each order daily or weekly time in tradition-specific ways.
African indigenous rites are diverse and often link community life to ancestors, seasons and life stages.
Comparison should respect differences and avoid making one tradition the standard.

en.title: Ethics and Morality in the Religions: Duty, Virtue, Love and Law
en.short: How religions ground duty, virtue, love and law, and where their moral rules differ.

sections.heading: Four ways of grounding ethics
sections.text: Religious ethics asks what acts are right and what kind of person to become. Deontology holds that duties bind whatever the outcome. Virtue ethics asks about character and practical wisdom (phronesis). Divine command theory says an act is right because God commands it, and faces the Euthyphro problem: is the good good because God wills it, or does God will it because it is good? Natural law theory holds that reason can read moral ends from human nature.

sections.heading: Law, duty and community
sections.text: Judaism grounds much ethics in halakha, the path of commandments (mitzvot) interpreted by rabbis. Islam grounds ethics in sharia, whose classical sources include the Qur’an, the sunna (the Prophet’s practice), analogy (qiyas) and consensus (ijma); schools of law differ in detail. Hindu and Buddhist ethics speak of dharma, duty and order, with karma, the moral law of cause and effect, and ahimsa, non-harm. Confucian ethics centres on li, ritual propriety, and ren, humaneness, aiming at the junzi, the exemplary person. Many African traditions stress communal personhood, as in ubuntu.

sections.heading: Love and virtue
sections.text: Christian ethics gives a central place to agape, self-giving love; Aquinas held that law is fulfilled in love. Buddhist ethics cultivates karuna, compassion, and metta, loving-kindness. Traditions usually combine these patterns: Islamic law also praises virtues, and Confucian ritual also expresses affection.

sections.heading: Contested issues
sections.text:
On honesty, traditions agree but differ on exceptions, such as when silence may protect life. On sexuality, most traditional teachings restrict sexual acts to marriage between a man and a woman, while some denominations and reform movements dissent; check current statements. On family, filial duty appears in Confucian, Jewish, Islamic and Christian teaching. On the environment, Judaism and Christianity offer stewardship, Islam trusteeship (khalifa), Hindu and Buddhist thought non-harm and interdependence.

A case: a trader is offered a loan at interest. A Muslim scholar may hold riba (interest) forbidden; a Kantian asks whether the practice can be universalised; a Christian asks what love of neighbour requires. Grounds differ, and sometimes conclusions.

keyPoints: Deontology, virtue ethics, divine command theory and natural law are four ways of grounding moral rules.
Judaism works through halakha and Islam through sharia, whose schools differ in detail.
Hindu and Buddhist ethics use dharma, karma and ahimsa; Confucian ethics uses li and ren.
Christian ethics centres on agape, and Buddhist ethics on karuna and metta.
Traditions usually combine law, virtue and love rather than relying on one alone.
On sexuality and other contested issues, traditions differ internally; check each body’s current teaching.

en.title: Philosophy of Religion: Arguments and Problems
en.short: Arguments for God, the problem of evil, faith and reason, religious language, miracles and afterlife.

sections.heading: Arguments for God
sections.text: The cosmological argument reasons from contingency or change to a first cause. Aquinas’s “Five Ways” include classic versions; David Hume and Immanuel Kant raised objections. The teleological argument, or argument from design, reasons from order or purpose to a designer. William Paley’s watch analogy is famous; Darwinian evolution and Hume’s critique of analogy are standard replies. The ontological argument moves from the concept of God to God’s existence. Anselm’s version defines God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived; Kant argued that existence is not a predicate. Each argument has defenders and critics.

sections.heading: Problem of Evil
sections.text: The problem of evil asks how an all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good God can coexist with evil. The logical form claims this is contradictory; the evidential form claims evil makes belief unlikely. A theodicy tries to justify God’s ways; a defence only shows possible consistency. Free-will, soul-making and greater-good responses are debated. Case: a flood destroys a village. A critic says natural evil is pointless; a defender may reply that unknown goods or human response could justify it. Neither side is settled.

sections.heading: Faith and Reason
sections.text: Faith and reason asks whether religious belief should rest on evidence, trust or both. Evidentialism holds that belief needs proportioned evidence; fideism stresses faith beyond reason; reformed epistemology argues belief in God may be properly basic, not inferred. Natural theology seeks rational support; Barthian and other views stress revelation. Philosophers disagree, so describe positions rather than settle them.

sections.heading: Language, Miracles, Afterlife
sections.text: Religious language debates ask whether talk of God is literal, analogical or symbolic. A miracle is often defined as an extraordinary event that breaks a natural law, attributed to divine action; Hume argued testimony for miracles is weak because natural laws are well established. Life after death raises questions about personal identity: what makes a resurrected or reincarnated person the same person? Traditions answer differently, and philosophy tests coherence.

keyPoints: Cosmological arguments infer God from contingency or change; teleological arguments infer a designer from order; ontological arguments infer existence from the concept of God.
Each argument has serious objections, including Hume’s and Kant’s, so none settles the question by itself.
The problem of evil challenges belief in an all-powerful, all-good God; defences and theodicies reply in different ways.
Faith and reason positions range from evidentialism to fideism and reformed epistemology.
Religious language may be read literally, analogically or symbolically.
Hume’s critique of miracle testimony and puzzles about personal identity shape debates on miracles and life after death.

en.title: Religion and Politics: State, Power and Conflict
en.short: Church and state, secularism, theocracy, religious nationalism, fundamentalism, and cases in Nigeria and India.

sections.heading: Church and state
sections.text: Church and state relations describe how religious bodies and political authority share, divide or contest power. The word church here means organised religion generally, not only Christianity. Three broad models appear in textbooks: union, where one religion is fused with the state; separation, where each has its own sphere; and accommodation, where the state supports religion without establishing one. Real cases usually mix these.

sections.heading: Secularism and theocracy
sections.text: Secularism is the principle that the state should be neutral between religions, or separate from them, so that citizenship does not depend on faith. It takes different forms: France’s laicite restricts public religious signs, while the United States bars an established church but protects free exercise. Theocracy is rule in the name of a religion or by religious authorities; Iran is often described as a theocratic republic. Neither term is simply the absence or presence of religion in public life.

sections.heading: Nationalism and fundamentalism
sections.text: Religious nationalism ties national identity to a religion, so that one faith defines the nation and minorities may be treated as outsiders. Fundamentalism is a modern, organised effort to return to what followers see as founding truths, often in reaction to secularisation; it is not the same as all traditional or conservative religion. Both can be peaceful or can justify coercion, depending on groups and context.

sections.heading: Nigeria, India and peace
sections.text: Nigeria’s constitution bars the federal or state government from adopting a state religion, yet religion shapes elections, law and conflict. Some northern states apply Islamic law in personal and criminal matters for Muslims, and the Boko Haram insurgency rejects the secular state. India’s constitution does not establish a state religion and protects freedom of religion. Hindu nationalism, or Hindutva, has grown politically, and the Ayodhya dispute over a mosque and temple site has been central; the Supreme Court awarded the site for a temple and separate land for a mosque in 2019. Peacebuilding uses interfaith dialogue, mediation by religious and traditional leaders, constitutional courts and civil society to reduce violence and negotiate shared public space.

keyPoints: Church and state relations can be union, separation or accommodation, and real cases mix them.
Secularism means state neutrality or separation, not the absence of religion from society.
Theocracy is rule by or in the name of religious authority.
Religious nationalism links national identity to one faith and can marginalise minorities.
Fundamentalism is a modern, organised claim to recover founding truths, not all conservative religion.
Nigeria and India show constitutional secularism under pressure, and peacebuilding uses dialogue, courts and mediation.

en.title: Religion, Law and Human Rights
en.short: Religious law, state law, freedom of religion and group versus individual rights.

sections.heading: Religious and state law
sections.text: Religious law is norms a community treats as sacred or divinely grounded. Halakha is Jewish law, developed from the Torah and rabbinic interpretation. Sharia is Islamic law, drawn from the Qur’an, the Sunna (the Prophet Muhammad’s example) and juristic reasoning; its schools and state applications differ. Canon law is a church’s internal law, especially the Catholic Church’s, governing worship, clergy and membership. State law is made or recognised by political authority and enforced by courts. States may adopt, recognise or ignore religious law.

sections.heading: Legal pluralism
sections.text: Legal pluralism means more than one legal order operates in society. Scope varies by country. Israel gives rabbinical courts jurisdiction over marriage and divorce for Jews, while general law remains secular. India retains separate personal laws for religious communities; its constitution’s directive principles call for a uniform civil code, and reform is debated. In Nigeria, the constitution guarantees freedom of religion, while some northern states apply sharia, mainly for Muslims, in personal and some criminal matters; this is contested. A secular state may leave religious law morally binding but unenforced by its courts.

sections.heading: Freedom of belief
sections.text: Freedom of religion or belief is the right to hold, change and manifest a religion or belief, alone or with others, publicly or privately. Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects it. The inner freedom to believe is absolute. Manifestation may be limited by law only where necessary to protect public safety, order, health, morals or others’ rights. Limits must be proportionate and non-discriminatory. States apply them differently.

sections.heading: Group and individual rights
sections.text: Group rights protect a community’s ability to practise and manage its affairs. Individual rights protect each member’s conscience and equality. They clash when a religious court or custom treats women or minorities unequally. In an invented case, Amina seeks a divorce her husband can obtain more easily. A civil court may offer an equal remedy, but the community may see this as interference. Some states reform religious law, some allow civil alternatives, and some defer to religious authorities.

keyPoints: Religious law is treated by a community as sacred or divinely grounded, while state law is made or recognised by political authority and enforced by courts.
Halakha, sharia and canon law are internally diverse and are recognised by states in different ways.
Legal pluralism means that more than one legal order operates in a society, and its scope varies by country.
Freedom of religion or belief protects inner belief absolutely and protects manifestation with limited, proportionate restrictions.
Group rights and individual rights can clash over religious courts, custom and equality.
States balance these claims differently, through reform, civil alternatives or deference to religious authorities.

en.title: Interfaith Dialogue and Religious Pluralism
en.short: Dialogue, debate and proclamation, exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism, and conversion ethics.

sections.heading: Three modes
sections.text: Dialogue is conversation between different traditions for mutual understanding. Participants listen and expect to learn; they do not aim to win. Debate is competitive: each side defends a position and tries to persuade. It can be respectful, but its purpose is proof or victory. Proclamation is a declaration of a tradition’s message, such as evangelism or da’wah (invitation to Islam). It differs from dialogue, which requires both sides to consent to an equal exchange.

sections.heading: Theologies of diversity
sections.text: Theologies of diversity are often grouped in three ways. Exclusivism holds that salvation or final truth is found only through one tradition; others may teach moral truths but are not seen as saving. Inclusivism holds that one tradition is normative, yet divine grace or truth can reach people outside it. Pluralism holds that religions are different valid responses to ultimate reality, so no single tradition possesses all truth. This typology is a tool; traditions vary internally and some believers reject these labels.

sections.heading: Dialogue in practice
sections.text: In practice, dialogue takes theological, ethical, spiritual and everyday forms. Theological dialogue compares beliefs and texts. Ethical dialogue joins shared action, such as disaster relief or a clinic. Everyday dialogue is neighbourly conversation. Good practice needs equal footing, a clear purpose, confidentiality where agreed, and freedom to disagree. For example, a church and a mosque might jointly run a clinic. They agree staff will not persuade patients; faith is explained only if a patient asks. If a volunteer breaks this, the committee reviews it.

sections.heading: Conversion ethics
sections.text: Conversion raises ethical questions. Freedom of religion or belief protects the right to change, keep or reject a faith; legal details vary by country. Persuasion should be honest and non-coercive, without exploiting illness, poverty, age or dependence. Dialogue groups often agree that no one will be pressured to convert and that conversion is not a hidden aim. Proclamation remains permitted in many legal systems, but it should respect consent, privacy and equal dignity. The line between witness and manipulation is debated; state the policy openly.

keyPoints: Dialogue seeks mutual understanding; debate seeks to persuade or win; proclamation declares a tradition’s message.
Exclusivism holds that salvation or final truth is found only in one tradition.
Inclusivism holds that one tradition is normative but divine grace or truth can reach others.
Pluralism holds that religions are different valid responses to ultimate reality.
Good dialogue needs equal footing, a clear purpose and freedom to disagree.
Conversion ethics requires honesty, non-coercion and respect for freedom of religion or belief, whose legal details vary by country.

en.title: Religion and Science: Conflict, Independence and Dialogue
en.short: Conflict, independence and dialogue models, with Galileo, Darwin, creationism and intelligent design.

sections.heading: Three models
sections.text: Ian Barbour, in Religion and Science (1997), offered a widely used typology, meaning a simple classification. Conflict holds that science and religion make rival claims about the same questions, so one must give way. Independence holds that they answer different questions: science describes what is, religion addresses meaning and value. Stephen Jay Gould called this non-overlapping magisteria. Dialogue looks for real conversation about method, ethics or the limits of each. Barbour added integration, where the two are combined. These are analytical tools, not the official position of any tradition.

sections.heading: The Galileo affair
sections.text: Galileo Galilei defended heliocentrism, the claim that the Earth orbits the Sun. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him, found him vehemently suspected of heresy, a formal finding short of conviction, and put him under house arrest. Popular accounts call this science against religion. Historians reply that the dispute also involved scriptural authority, academic rivalry and papal politics, and that Galileo had clerical supporters. In 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged errors in the Church’s handling of the case. The episode shows how an institutional clash can look like a clash of ideas.

sections.heading: Darwin and after
sections.text: Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) argued that species change by natural selection. Christian responses ranged from acceptance to rejection, and still do. Young-earth creationists read Genesis as teaching a recent creation in six days. Old-earth creationists accept geological time but not common descent, the idea that all species share ancestors. Intelligent design, associated with Michael Behe, argues that some biological systems are too complex to have evolved and point to a designer; critics answer that the claim is not testable. In the United States, a federal court ruled in Kitzmiller v. Dover (2005) that intelligent design is not science and cannot be taught as science in public school science classes.

sections.heading: Current debate
sections.text: Debate now turns on specific claims rather than a general war: the age of the Earth, evolutionary accounts of human behaviour, climate change and biotechnology. Positions vary by country and by tradition, and many scientists are religious. Check the current official statements of the body concerned.

keyPoints: Barbour’s typology distinguishes conflict, independence, dialogue and integration.
The conflict model treats science and religion as rivals over the same questions.
The Galileo affair involved scriptural authority and church politics as well as astronomy.
Darwinian evolution drew mixed religious responses, and still does.
Young-earth creationism, old-earth creationism and intelligent design are distinct positions.
In Kitzmiller v. Dover (2005) a US federal court ruled that intelligent design is not science for public school science classes.

en.title: Religion, Development and the Environment
en.short: Faith-based development in Africa and Asia, creation care, stewardship and the environmental debate.

sections.heading: Faith-based development
sections.text:
Faith-based organisations (FBOs) are charities, clinics, schools or relief agencies linked to a religious community. In Africa and Asia they often run hospitals, teacher training, orphan care, food distribution and disaster relief. Their religious identity can build trust, reach remote areas and mobilise volunteers and donations. It can also shape priorities, for example by favouring members of one faith or by attaching prayer to services. Accountability matters: FBOs should report spending and results to donors, governments and the people they serve.

An invented example: a church clinic in rural Tanzania offers maternal care and a mosque-run school in Kano, Nigeria, teaches literacy; both keep public records and work with local health or education authorities.

sections.heading: Creation care
sections.text: Creation care is religiously motivated action to protect the natural world. Stewardship means humans hold the earth in trust for God or for future generations, not as owners. Many traditions contain such teaching: Jewish and Christian readings of Genesis, the Islamic idea of khalifa (trusteeship), and Hindu and Buddhist emphasis on ahimsa (non-harm) and interdependence. Interpretations differ. Some read dominion in Genesis as a licence to use nature; others read it as responsible care. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato si' (2015) is a prominent Catholic statement on ecology.

sections.heading: The debate
sections.text: Does religion help or hinder environmental action? Supporters point to moral motivation, community trust, long-term presence and simple-living ideals. FBOs can mobilise tree planting, water projects and climate adaptation where states are weak. Critics point to otherworldly teaching that devalues the earth, anthropocentrism (human-centredness), suspicion of environmental science, and ties to logging, mining or large families. Historian Lynn White Jr (1967) argued that Western Christianity helped cause the ecological crisis; many scholars reply that he ignored other readings and traditions. Evidence is mixed and context-specific. The debate is not settled, and the same tradition can supply both care and neglect.

keyPoints: Faith-based organisations run health, education and relief work in Africa and Asia, and their religious identity can build trust but also shape who is served.
Creation care is religiously motivated environmental protection; stewardship means humans hold the earth in trust rather than owning it.
Traditions differ: Genesis dominion, Islamic khalifa and Hindu or Buddhist ahimsa can all be read as supporting care for nature.
Lynn White Jr (1967) argued that Western Christianity contributed to the ecological crisis, but many scholars call his thesis oversimplified.
Religion can help environmental action through moral motivation and community networks, and hinder it through anthropocentrism or suspicion of science.
The evidence is mixed and context-specific, so general claims that religion either saves or wrecks the environment should be avoided.

en.title: Religion, Gender and Sexuality
en.short: Gender roles, family, feminist readings of scripture, ordination and sexuality across traditions.

sections.heading: Terms and approach
sections.text: Gender here means the roles a society assigns to women and men; sex means biological features. The two are often distinguished, though traditions differ on how far roles are fixed by nature. Scholars ask what scriptures and customs say, who is allowed to interpret them, and whose voices are heard. Because interpretation shapes practice, a text’s meaning for gender is argued over rather than simply read off.

sections.heading: Women, men and family
sections.text: Most traditions treat the household as a basic unit of religious life. Christian teaching often pictures marriage as a covenant; Jewish law, like Islamic law, treats marriage as a contract with rights and duties for each spouse; Confucian thought orders family relations by role and seniority. Many traditions give men public leadership in worship while honouring women’s religious authority in the home. Practice varies by country and class, so broad statements need care.

sections.heading: Feminist readings
sections.text: Feminist readings ask whether a text reflects its patriarchal setting or carries a liberating strand within it. Some scholars use a hermeneutic of suspicion, which means reading with attention to androcentric (male-centred) language and to what has been left out. Others retrieve overlooked women. Examples include Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza on early Christianity, Phyllis Trible on Hebrew narrative, Judith Plaskow on Judaism, and Amina Wadud and Asma Barlas on the Qur’an. Reformist readings reach different conclusions, so the argument is internal to each tradition.

sections.heading: Ordination and sexuality
sections.text: Ordination is the formal setting apart of clergy. The Roman Catholic Church and the Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests; among Anglicans and Protestants practice differs by province or denomination. Reform and Conservative Judaism ordain women rabbis; Orthodox Judaism does not. On sexuality, most traditional jurisprudence allows sexual relations only within heterosexual marriage, while some Protestant churches and liberal Jewish movements now bless same-sex unions. In Nigeria, the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 criminalises same-sex marriage, showing how law and religion interact.

keyPoints: Gender names socially assigned roles; sex names biological features, and traditions differ on how far roles are fixed by nature.
Marriage is a covenant in much Christian teaching and a contract in Jewish and Islamic law, with duties assigned to each spouse.
Feminist hermeneutics divides between suspicion of patriarchal texts and retrieval of liberating strands.
The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches reserve priesthood to men, while Anglican and Protestant practice varies.
Reform and Conservative Judaism ordain women rabbis; Orthodox Judaism does not.
Most traditional jurisprudence restricts sexual relations to heterosexual marriage, and Nigeria’s 2013 Act shows law and religion interacting.

en.title: Religion in Nigeria: History and Contemporary Issues
en.short: Indigenous religion, Islam and Christianity in Nigeria, Sharia, conflict and peacebuilding.

sections.heading: Three religious streams
sections.text: Indigenous traditions are the oldest layer: belief in a supreme being, veneration of divinities and ancestors, and shrines, varying from community to community. Islam crossed the Sahara through trade and scholars, reaching Kanem-Bornu by about the eleventh century and Hausaland mainly from the fourteenth century. Christianity arrived with Portuguese Catholic missions in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries at Benin and Warri, and expanded in the nineteenth century through societies such as the Church Missionary Society and Catholic orders, and through African agents such as Samuel Ajayi Crowther.

sections.heading: Caliphate and missions
sections.text: In 1804 Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar, led a reform movement in Hausaland. His followers built the Sokoto Caliphate, which bound emirates to a caliph and promoted Maliki law and Sufi brotherhoods. British conquest in 1903 ended the caliphate, but emirs kept religious authority. Missions founded schools and hospitals. In the twentieth century independent Aladura churches (Yoruba for 'people of prayer') broke away, and Pentecostal churches grew fast from the 1970s, drawing students and urban migrants.

sections.heading: Sharia and conflict
