sections.text: From 1999 a group of northern states, commonly counted as twelve, extended Sharia from personal matters to criminal law. Supporters presented it as justice and identity; critics argued that it clashed with constitutional guarantees of freedom of religion and with the rights of non-Muslims. The 1999 Constitution bars federal and state governments from adopting a religion as the state religion. Tensions have flared in cities such as Jos and Kaduna, and the Boko Haram insurgency, which began in Maiduguri, has caused heavy loss of life.

sections.heading: Peacebuilding
sections.text: The Nigerian Inter-Religious Council (NIREC), formed in 1999, brings Christian and Muslim leaders together. It is co-chaired by the Sultan of Sokoto and the president of the Christian Association of Nigeria, and it mediates disputes, issues joint statements and supports dialogue. State peace commissions, women’s and youth groups and NGOs also do early warning, mediation and reconstruction work. Researchers disagree about how far these bodies reduce violence.

keyPoints: Indigenous traditions, Islam and Christianity all have long histories in Nigeria.
Islam spread across the Sahara from about the eleventh century; Portuguese Catholic missions came in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
The Sokoto Caliphate, built after Usman dan Fodio’s 1804 movement, shaped law and authority in the north.
From 1999 several northern states extended Sharia to criminal matters, which supporters saw as justice and critics as a clash with constitutional religious freedom.
Pentecostal churches grew rapidly from the 1970s, alongside older Aladura independent churches.
NIREC, formed in 1999, is co-chaired by the Sultan of Sokoto and the Christian Association of Nigeria president and works on mediation and dialogue.

en.title: Research Methods in Religious Studies: Questions, Sources and Ethics
en.short: Framing research questions, reviewing literature, using library, archival and field sources, ethics and writing a proposal.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question states what you want to find out and why it matters. It should be narrow enough to answer with the time and sources you have, and open enough to allow evidence to change your view. Turn a topic into a question: not “religion and migration” but “how do migrant churches in Lagos support new arrivals?” Check feasibility, access and ethics before committing.

sections.heading: Reviewing literature
sections.text: A literature review maps what scholars already know and where they disagree. Search library catalogues, journal databases and bibliographies; record search terms and results so the work can be checked. Read primary sources (original documents or data) and secondary sources (later analysis), and distinguish description from argument. The review should identify a gap or a debate your project can address, not just list summaries.

sections.heading: Sources and fieldwork
sections.text: Library sources include books, journals and reference works. Archives hold documents, letters, minutes and audio recordings; access rules and catalogues vary, so ask the archivist. Ethnography means long-term observation and participation in a community. Interviews can be structured, semi-structured or open. In a small case, a student studying Friday prayers at a Lagos mosque might observe, interview the imam (prayer leader) and worshippers with permission, and compare notes with published work. Triangulation means checking a finding against more than one source.

sections.heading: Ethics, citation and writing
sections.text: Fieldwork ethics require informed consent, meaning participants agree freely after understanding the study, voluntary participation, no harm, confidentiality and secure data storage. Seek permission from community leaders and follow local norms; discuss how findings will be shared. Reflexivity means reflecting on how your own position shapes the research. Cite every source in the style your department requires, such as APA, Chicago or Harvard, and keep a reference list. A proposal usually states the question, rationale, literature review, methods, ethics, timeline and limits. The final project adds findings, analysis and honest discussion of limitations.

keyPoints: A good research question is narrow, answerable, ethical and connected to a scholarly debate.
A literature review identifies a gap or disagreement, not just a list of summaries.
Library, archival, ethnographic and interview sources each need checking and triangulation.
Fieldwork with living communities requires informed consent, confidentiality, permissions and respect for local norms.
Citation must follow your department’s style and every borrowed idea must be credited.
A proposal sets out question, methods, ethics, timeline and limits; the final project reports findings and limitations.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Religion: Practice, Cognition and Critique
en.short: Lived and material religion, embodied practice, cognitive and evolutionary accounts, and postcolonial critique.

sections.heading: Lived and material
sections.text: Lived religion studies what people actually do and feel in everyday life, not only official doctrine. It asks how practice, memory and community shape belief. Material religion extends this to bodies, buildings, images, dress, sound, food and space. A researcher might study a mosque in Kano by observing washing, shoe removal, crowding, sermon sound and the route home. Such detail shows religion as made and remade, though critics warn that everyday practice can be described without explaining change or power.

sections.heading: Embodied and cognitive
sections.text: Embodied practice treats knowledge as learned through posture, gesture, rhythm and training. A worshipper’s bow or a healer’s touch is not decoration; it forms attention and memory. Cognitive science of religion asks which ordinary mental capacities make religious ideas easy to learn and spread. Examples include agency detection, the tendency to see agents even where none exist, and theory of mind, the ability to infer others’ thoughts. Evolutionary accounts ask whether religion is an adaptation, a by-product of other capacities, or both. They disagree, and each needs evidence from more than one culture.

sections.heading: Postcolonial critique
sections.text: Postcolonial critique examines how colonial power shaped the study of religion. Talal Asad argues that the modern category of religion, separated from politics and law, is historically Christian and not neutral. Tomoko Masuzawa argues that the world religions paradigm, the approach that sorts traditions into a list of major faiths, ranks them in a hierarchy. Decolonial critique goes further, asking whose languages, archives and questions set the terms. It warns that classifying African or Asian practice as 'religion' may distort it. The critique is strong on power and history, but it can leave researchers without usable categories; the task is to use categories critically.

sections.heading: Evaluating theory
sections.text: No single theory explains religion completely. Lived and material approaches are strong on detail but weak on comparison. Cognitive and evolutionary accounts are testable but can reduce religion to mind or biology. Postcolonial critique guards against universal claims. Good research combines methods and states its limits.

keyPoints: Lived religion studies everyday practice and meaning, not only official doctrine.
Material religion analyses bodies, objects, buildings, sound and space.
Embodied practice treats knowledge as formed through posture, gesture and training.
Cognitive and evolutionary accounts ask how ordinary mental capacities and selection pressures shape religious ideas, but they disagree on adaptation versus by-product.
Postcolonial and decolonial critiques argue that 'religion' and the world religions paradigm carry colonial and Christian assumptions.
No single theory is complete; good research combines methods and states its limits.

en.title: Comparative Religion: Methods and Debates
en.short: How scholars compare religions, the insider/outsider problem, controlled comparison and its critics.

sections.heading: Why compare
sections.text: Comparative religion is the systematic study of similarities and differences between traditions. It is a method, not a separate religion. Nineteenth-century scholars such as F. Max Müller treated it as a science of religion, and many early comparisons ranked traditions on a ladder from primitive to advanced. That ranking is now rejected as unjustified and colonial in origin. Comparison survives as a tool for asking questions, not for grading.

sections.heading: Insider and outsider
sections.text: Two terms borrowed from linguistics name the problem: emic (the insider’s own categories) and etic (the analyst’s categories). A practitioner may say she talks to God; the analyst may call it petitionary prayer. Neither account is simply wrong, but they answer different questions, so mixing them produces false matches. Talal Asad argued in Genealogies of Religion (1993) that religion itself is a modern Western category, so comparison can carry Christian assumptions into the data. Translation is part of the method, not a step before it.

sections.heading: Controlled comparison
sections.text: A controlled comparison states its tertium comparationis, the shared ground of comparison, then holds some features constant and varies others. Take fasting. Ramadan, in Islam, is a month of daytime abstinence; the fast itself is, in Sunni Islam, one of the Five Pillars, obligatory for most adults. Lent, in Christianity, is a penitential season of about forty days; it is not a pillar, and its rules differ by church and country. The shared word hides different functions: communal obligation in one case, penitential discipline in the other. The comparison sharpens a question rather than yielding a law.

sections.heading: Assessing the results
sections.text: Results are judged by whether the tertium comparationis is defensible, whether context is respected, and whether the comparison explains something the single case did not. Critics of the world religions scheme, such as Tomoko Masuzawa in The Invention of World Religions (2005), show that the standard list of major religions is a historical product. Comparison remains useful for typology and hypotheses, not for ranking.

keyPoints: Comparison is a method for asking questions, not for ranking traditions.
Emic means insider categories and etic means analyst categories; mixing them produces false matches.
A controlled comparison must state its tertium comparationis, the shared ground being compared.
Comparing Ramadan and Lent shows that one word, fasting, can cover different functions.
Jonathan Z. Smith treats comparison as the scholar’s own act, not a fact found in the data.
The list of world religions is a historical product, so results must be checked against context.

en.title: Dissertation Methods in Religious Studies
en.short: Scoping literature, design, ethics, texts or communities, analysis, writing, supervision and viva.

sections.heading: Scoping and design
sections.text:
Begin with a question narrow enough for a master’s dissertation. A scoping review maps the debates, sources and methods; it is not a list of summaries, and it should show the gap you address. Research design is the plan linking question, evidence and methods. You may use texts, interviews, observation or surveys, but justify the choice and state its limits.

For example, a student studying how young Muslims in Kano use online sermons might combine interviews with analysis of sermons, limiting period and preachers.

sections.heading: Ethics and access
sections.text:
Obtain ethics approval from your institution’s committee before collecting data; rules differ by country and institution, so check requirements. Informed consent means clear information, voluntary participation and the right to withdraw. Protect identities through anonymisation, secure storage and care with quotations.

Community work needs gatekeepers’ permission, respect and reciprocity; avoid extracting stories and leaving. Textual work raises provenance, copyright, permissions and translation limits. Ask whether a participant or reader could be harmed by publication.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text:
Qualitative analysis begins with coding, labelling data segments, then comparing codes to build themes. Triangulation checks a finding against more than one source. Reflexivity examines how your position shapes the research. For texts, contextualise passages, compare versions and show interpretive steps.

Write an argument-led thesis: introduction, literature review, methods, findings, discussion, conclusion. Use a referencing style and record every source to avoid plagiarism. Originality can be a new question, case, synthesis or method application; it need not be grand theory.

sections.heading: Supervision and viva
sections.text:
Supervision is a working relationship, not a proofreading service. Agree a schedule, send written work before meetings and keep notes on decisions. Your supervisor advises; you remain responsible for the thesis. The viva is an oral examination by examiners who have read the dissertation.

Prepare a summary of your question, method, finding and contribution. Reread the thesis, mark weak points and hold a mock viva. Answer directly, give evidence and admit limits. Check institutional regulations for submission, word limits and viva format, if your programme holds one.

keyPoints: A master’s dissertation needs a narrow question and a scoping review that shows the gap.
Research design links the question to evidence and methods, and states limits.
Ethics approval and informed consent are required before data collection; rules vary by country and institution.
Coding, triangulation and reflexivity are basic tools for qualitative analysis.
Originality can be a new question, case, synthesis or method application, not only a new theory.
The viva is an oral defence: summarise your argument, evidence and limits, and check institutional rules.

en.title: Religion, Media and Globalisation: A Frontier Topic
en.short: Religion in film, print, broadcast and digital media; globalisation, diaspora, Pentecostal and Islamic media.

sections.heading: Media and religion
sections.text: Media are the channels through which religion is carried: print, film, broadcast and digital platforms. Studying religion and media means asking who produces the content, who controls it, and how audiences receive it. Mediatisation is the argument that institutions, religious ones included, increasingly take on the form and logic of media. Scholars debate whether this changes religion itself or only its publicity.

sections.heading: Film, print and broadcast
sections.text: Religious groups have long used print, radio and television to spread teaching. Pentecostal media is a large research field: megachurches broadcast services, sell recordings and build audiences across borders. Islamic media range from satellite preachers to online Qur’an recitation and fatwa sites, which publish scholars’ rulings on Islamic law. Researchers ask whether such media widen access or concentrate authority in a few popular preachers. Findings vary by country, so read local studies.

sections.heading: Digital worship and authority
sections.text: Digital media change worship when services are streamed, prayers are offered in chat groups and rituals are performed at a distance. Authority shifts as well: a scholar’s ruling may circulate online without the local body that once approved it. Community can become looser and wider, linking diaspora members to a home congregation. A small case: a Lagos church streams its Sunday service; members in London join live, give online and run a WhatsApp prayer group. Attendance is easy to count; belonging is not.

sections.heading: Globalisation and diaspora
sections.text: Globalisation is the growing flow of people, money, images and ideas across borders. Migration produces diaspora religions, where communities keep practice alive away from their place of origin and adapt it to a new setting. Second-generation members often practise differently from their parents. Pentecostal and Islamic media are current research frontiers because they cross borders quickly. Scholars use the terms diaspora and globalisation in different ways, so define them in your own work.

keyPoints: Media studies of religion ask who produces content, who controls it and how audiences receive it.
Mediatisation is the claim that institutions increasingly take the form and logic of media.
Pentecostal and Islamic media are active research frontiers in several countries.
Digital media reshape worship, authority and community, not only publicity.
Diaspora religions keep practice alive away from the place of origin and adapt it.
Define contested terms such as diaspora and globalisation in your own writing.
